stem: A 58-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes has had three Candida infections in two years, including esophagitis, but no deep bacterial infections. A nitroblue tetrazolium test on her neutrophils is normal, but a myeloperoxidase stain shows no enzyme in her neutrophils. Consider the sequence of oxidants made during the neutrophil respiratory burst.
oneliner: 58F + diabetes + recurrent Candida, no deep bacterial infections + normal NBT + absent MPO stain → which oxidant is missing?
ask: Which oxidant product is absent from her neutrophils?

whyNot.A: Made by NADPH oxidase **before** the block; the **normal NBT test** shows this step works
whyNot.B: Made from superoxide by dismutase, **upstream** of myeloperoxidase; it is still produced (and in fact accumulates)
whyNot.C: Formed from H2O2 by **iron (Fenton reaction)**, which needs no myeloperoxidase; the **normal NBT** shows the H2O2 supply is intact
whyNot.E: Made by **iNOS**, a separate pathway that does not depend on myeloperoxidase

answer: Hypochlorous acid (bleach), because myeloperoxidase is absent
why: The burst runs in order: NADPH oxidase makes **superoxide**, dismutase turns it into **hydrogen peroxide**, and **myeloperoxidase** uses H2O2 plus chloride to make **hypochlorous acid**. A block removes only the products **after** it. A **normal NBT** places the defect beyond the oxidase, and **absent MPO** removes only bleach; residual H2O2 explains why the course is mild, with Candida the main problem.
chain: Phagocytosis triggers NADPH oxidase: superoxide made (NBT normal)
Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to H2O2
Myeloperoxidase needed to join H2O2 with chloride
Enzyme absent, so no hypochlorous acid
H2O2 still kills most bacteria; Candida escapes more easily

idea.rule: In a linear pathway, a block removes only what comes after it; the steps before it still work or pile up.
also: Chronic granulomatous disease: oxidase block, so no superoxide and no downstream oxidants (NBT abnormal)
Galactosemia: galactose-1-phosphate piles up behind the blocked uridyltransferase
Phenylketonuria: phenylalanine piles up behind the blocked hydroxylase
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase): precursors pile up and shunt to androgens

note: Plan topic was T-IM-CGD; changed to T-IM-MPODEF because the case is myeloperoxidase deficiency. NBT only (not DHR), since DHR oxidation is MPO-dependent and can look abnormal in MPO deficiency. Review: option C NADPH (a substrate, not an oxidant) replaced by hydroxyl radical.

stem: In a vaccine trial, healthy adult volunteers receive killed Vibrio cholerae either orally or by intramuscular injection. Only the oral group develops antigen-specific antibody in stool. That antibody is a dimer joined by a J chain and carries a secretory component acquired during transport across the epithelium. It does not cross the placenta.
oneliner: Healthy volunteers + oral (not IM) killed cholera vaccine + stool antibody that is a J-chain dimer with secretory component → main protective action?
ask: What is the main way this antibody protects the gut when cholera later arrives?

options.A: Activating the classical complement pathway on the bacterial surface
options.B: Blocking attachment of bacteria and toxin to the epithelium
options.C: Opsonizing bacteria for uptake by neutrophils
options.D: Binding Fc receptors on NK cells to drive killing of infected cells
options.E: Sensitizing mast cells to degranulate on re-exposure

whyNot.A: This antibody is a **poor** complement activator; classical activation is a job for **IgM and IgG**
whyNot.C: Opsonization works through **IgG** and Fc-gamma receptors; the **secretory component** is not an opsonin handle
whyNot.D: **ADCC** uses **IgG** bound to CD16; vibrios are extracellular and not NK targets
whyNot.E: Mast cell sensitization is **IgE**, which is not a dimer and is not found in stool

answer: Neutralization: it blocks microbes and toxin from attaching to the epithelium (immune exclusion)
why: The **J-chain dimer with secretory component** is **secretory IgA**, made by plasma cells in the lamina propria and transported across epithelium. Its main job is **immune exclusion**: it coats bacteria and toxin so they cannot **adhere** to mucosa, without causing inflammation. An **injected** vaccine mainly makes IgG, which is why it protects the gut poorly.
chain: Oral antigen sampled by M cells in Peyer patches
B cells switch to IgA there (TGF-beta) and settle in the lamina propria as plasma cells
Dimeric IgA (J chain) binds the poly-Ig receptor and is carried across the epithelium, keeping secretory component
Secretory IgA coats toxin and vibrios in the lumen
Attachment to epithelium blocked; the injected vaccine makes mainly IgG instead

idea.rule: Secretory IgA protects surfaces by blocking attachment (neutralization), not by opsonization or complement.
also: Breast milk IgA gives passive gut protection to the infant
Oral polio and cholera vaccines are used to induce mucosal IgA
IgA protease is a virulence factor of Neisseria, Haemophilus and Streptococcus pneumoniae
IgG, not IgA, crosses the placenta and opsonizes

stem: A 35-year-old Black woman has 3 months of cough and fatigue. Chest imaging shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and a biopsy of one node shows noncaseating granulomas. Her serum calcium is 11.4 mg/dL and her serum ACE level is raised. Consider how her calcium regulation differs from the normal state.
oneliner: 35F + bilateral hilar nodes + noncaseating granulomas + Ca 11.4 + raised ACE → which set of PTH, calcium, phosphate and calcitriol?
ask: Which set of changes best fits her mineral metabolism?

whyNot.A: This is **primary hyperparathyroidism**: PTH is raised and wastes phosphate; here granulomas, not a gland, drive the calcium
whyNot.B: This is the **PTHrP/malignancy** pattern; granulomas make **calcitriol**, so it is not low
whyNot.D: This is **chronic kidney disease**; she is **hypercalcemic**, not hypocalcemic
whyNot.E: This is **hypoparathyroidism**; her calcium is **high**, not low

why: Activated macrophages in **granulomas** express **1-alpha-hydroxylase** and make **calcitriol** without PTH control. It raises **gut absorption of calcium and phosphate**, so both rise, and the high calcium **suppresses PTH**. This is **non-PTH-mediated hypercalcemia** with a raised phosphate, unlike primary hyperparathyroidism.
chain: Granuloma macrophages make 1-alpha-hydroxylase
Calcitriol rises with no PTH feedback
Gut absorbs more calcium and phosphate
Serum calcium and phosphate both rise
High calcium suppresses PTH

idea.rule: Granulomas make calcitriol outside PTH control, so calcium and phosphate rise while PTH falls.
also: Tuberculosis granulomas can do the same
Lymphoma can produce extra calcitriol
Primary hyperparathyroidism: high PTH, low phosphate
Malignancy: PTHrP raises calcium but calcitriol stays low

note: Review: option E (labelled vitamin D deficiency with calcitriol ↑) was doubtful, since calcitriol is low or normal in that state; replaced by the hypoparathyroid pattern.

stem: In a culture experiment, human cells infected with a wild-type virus whose gene product lowers surface class I MHC are mixed with blood lymphocytes from a donor never exposed to the virus. The infected cells are lysed within hours, with release of perforin and granzymes, but CD8 T cells from the same donor do not kill them. Cells infected with a mutant virus that cannot lower class I MHC are spared.
oneliner: Experiment + virus lowers class I MHC on infected cells + unexposed donor lymphocytes kill them, CD8 T cells do not + mutant-virus cells spared → which interaction normally prevents killing?
ask: Which receptor-ligand interaction normally restrains the killer cells from attacking healthy cells?

options.A: T-cell receptor binding class I MHC-peptide
options.D: KIR binding self class I MHC

whyNot.A: This is how **CD8 T cells** get **activated**; with class I lost it fails, which is why they do nothing here
whyNot.B: A **costimulatory** signal for T cells, not an NK brake
whyNot.C: An **activating** pathway (ADCC) that needs **antibody**; an **unexposed donor** has none against this virus
whyNot.E: An **activating** receptor for stress ligands; it drives killing rather than restraining it

answer: KIR on the NK cell binding self class I MHC
why: The killers here are **NK cells**: they act without prior sensitization and use **perforin and granzymes**. Their activating signals are always present on stressed cells, but **KIR binding self class I MHC** delivers an **inhibitory** signal. When the virus removes class I, the **brake is lost** and the cell is killed, while CD8 T cells, which need class I, fail.
chain: Virus lowers class I MHC on infected cell
KIR on NK cell finds no self class I
Inhibitory signal lost; activating receptors dominate
Perforin and granzymes released, target killed
CD8 T cells cannot recognize the cell without class I

idea.rule: NK cells kill cells that lack self class I MHC (missing self); CD8 T cells kill cells that show it.
also: Tumors that lose class I MHC escape T cells but become NK targets
NK activation also uses CD16 (ADCC) and NKG2D (stress ligands)
IL-2, IL-12 and IFN-gamma activate NK cells
Perforin and granzymes are shared by NK cells and CD8 T cells

note: Review: mice changed to a human donor, because KIR is the human NK inhibitory receptor (mice use Ly49).

stem: A 13-year-old boy has acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The blasts express TdT but not surface CD3, CD4 or surface immunoglobulin, and resemble cortical thymocytes that have just begun to rearrange their T-cell receptor beta-chain gene. Consider the order of joining at this locus.
oneliner: 13M + ALL + TdT+, surface CD3-, CD4-, early cortical thymocyte starting TCR beta rearrangement → which joining comes first?
ask: Which gene-segment joining occurs first at this locus?

whyNot.A: V cannot join a **D** that is not yet next to a **J**; **D joins J first**
whyNot.C: Direct V to J is how **light chains and TCR alpha** are built; the beta locus has a **D** segment that is used first
whyNot.D: The constant region is joined by **RNA splicing**, not by DNA recombination
whyNot.E: **Beta rearranges first** and signals through pre-T-alpha before the alpha locus opens; these blasts are only **starting beta**

answer: D to J joining (then V to DJ)

shifts.var: D to J joining on the beta locus

why: Loci with a **D segment** (Ig heavy chain, TCR beta) join **D to J first** and then add **V to DJ**; loci without D (Ig light chains, TCR alpha) join **V to J** directly. **TdT** adds N-nucleotides at the joins, and **RAG1/RAG2** cut the DNA. Beta is rearranged **before** alpha in the thymus.
chain: RAG1/RAG2 recombinase active in early lymphocytes
D joins J on the beta locus
V then joins the DJ segment
TdT adds N-nucleotides at the joins
Beta chain pairs with pre-T-alpha before alpha rearranges

idea.rule: Heavy-chain and TCR beta loci join D-J first, then V-DJ; light chains and TCR alpha join V-J only.
also: Heavy chain rearranges before light chain in pre-B cells
RAG1/RAG2 deficiency causes SCID with no B or T cells
TdT is a marker for ALL blasts
Allelic exclusion lets each B cell express only one heavy-chain allele

note: Review: options made one shape (all named locus joinings); stem says surface CD3 (T-ALL blasts often carry cytoplasmic CD3); single shift.

stem: An 8-year-old girl is seen 1 hour after a cat scratched her forearm. Within a minute a red line formed along the scratch, followed by a warm red flush spreading around it; the skin is intact and not bleeding. Over the next 30 minutes the line became raised and swollen.
oneliner: 8F + cat scratch + red line and warm flush within a minute, skin intact, no bleeding + raised swelling by 30 min → what explains redness versus swelling?
ask: Which pair of vascular changes best explains the redness and then the swelling?

options.A: Redness from arteriolar dilation; swelling from venular endothelial gaps
options.B: Redness from capillary hemorrhage; swelling from venular endothelial gaps
options.C: Redness from arteriolar constriction; swelling from fibrin thrombi in venules
options.D: Redness from bacterial capillary congestion; swelling from arteriolar dilation alone
options.E: Redness from arteriolar dilation; swelling from fibrin thrombi in venules

whyNot.B: The skin is **intact with no bleeding**, so red streaks are not hemorrhage
whyNot.C: **Constriction** makes skin pale and cold, and lasts only seconds; this skin is **warm and red**
whyNot.D: Redness within **a minute** is too fast for bacterial effects, and arteriolar dilation alone raises flow without opening the **leak**
whyNot.E: Dilation is right, but swelling comes from **leaky venules** within an hour, not from thrombosis

answer: Histamine-driven arteriolar dilation (redness, heat), then venular endothelial gaps (fluid leak and swelling)
why: Injury gives a **brief arteriolar constriction**, then **histamine** from mast cells dilates arterioles, raising flow and causing **redness and heat**. **Histamine** also makes **venular endothelial cells contract**, opening **gaps** that let protein-rich fluid out, producing **swelling** within about 30 minutes.
chain: Mast cell histamine released at the injury
Arterioles dilate: more flow, redness and warmth
Venular endothelial cells contract, gaps open
Protein-rich fluid leaks into tissue
Local swelling (edema)

idea.rule: Acute inflammation: arteriolar dilation gives redness and heat; leaky venules give swelling.
also: Histamine, bradykinin and leukotrienes C4/D4/E4 raise vascular permeability
Leukocytes marginate and roll in venules, not arterioles
Exudate (protein-rich) versus transudate (protein-poor) separates inflammation from hydrostatic edema
Bee sting: local edema within 30 minutes by the same gaps

note: Review: 'red streaks' read as lymphangitis, so stem now describes the triple response; option A shortened to match the others (no 'histamine' giveaway).

stem: A 12-year-old girl has a knife laceration of the palm, repaired with sutures. On day 3 the wound shows a fibrin clot, neutrophils that are now fading, and abundant macrophages releasing growth factors.
oneliner: 12F + sutured palm laceration + day 3: fibrin clot, fading neutrophils, macrophages releasing growth factors → which phase comes next?

options.C: Remodeling (collagen III replaced by I, contraction)

whyNot.B: Occurs in the **first minutes**; the clot is already present
whyNot.C: A **late** phase after granulation tissue has formed, weeks to months
whyNot.D: **Already ending** here: neutrophils are fading and macrophages dominate
whyNot.E: Epithelial cover is only **part** of the next phase; the macrophage growth factors also act on **fibroblasts and vessels**

answer: Proliferation (fibroblasts, collagen, new vessels, granulation tissue)
why: Healing runs **hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, remodeling**. Macrophage-derived **growth factors (PDGF, TGF-beta, FGF, VEGF)** signal **fibroblasts and endothelium**, so the next phase is **proliferation**: fibroblasts lay down **type III collagen**, new capillaries form **granulation tissue**, and epithelium re-covers the wound.
chain: Platelet plug forms first
Neutrophils then macrophages clear debris
Macrophage growth factors stimulate fibroblasts and endothelium
Collagen III, new vessels, granulation tissue
Remodeling follows later

idea.rule: Wound healing order: hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, remodeling.
also: Granulation tissue = fibroblasts plus new capillaries
Type III collagen early, type I collagen in remodeling
Myofibroblasts cause wound contraction
Vitamin C and zinc are needed for collagen and healing

stem: A single B-cell clone secretes IgM against antigen X. After help from CD4 T cells through CD40-CD40L and IL-4, its daughter cells secrete IgE that binds antigen X with the same specificity and the same light chain.
oneliner: Experiment + B clone IgM to antigen X, then IgE with same specificity after CD4 help via CD40L and IL-4 → which domains changed?
ask: Which part of the immunoglobulin molecule was replaced?

whyNot.A: This **defines the antigen-binding site**, which is unchanged
whyNot.B: Also part of the **antigen-binding site**, unchanged
whyNot.D: The **light chain is identical** before and after the switch
whyNot.E: The antigen specificity is **the same**, so neither changed

why: **Class switching** swaps the **heavy-chain constant region** (via **AID**-mediated DNA recombination) so the same **VDJ** variable region joins a new **C gene** (gamma, alpha or epsilon). **CD40L on T cells** and **cytokines** (IL-4 for IgE/IgG4, IFN-gamma for IgG, TGF-beta for IgA) choose the isotype. **Specificity and light chain stay the same**.
chain: T-cell CD40L binds B-cell CD40
Cytokines pick the new C gene
AID deletes the Cmu region by switch recombination
Same VDJ joins a new constant gene
Same antigen specificity, new effector function

idea.rule: Class switching changes only the heavy-chain constant region; variable regions, light chain and specificity are unchanged.
also: CD40L (CD40LG) deficiency causes hyper-IgM syndrome
AID deficiency also blocks class switching and somatic hypermutation
Somatic hypermutation changes the variable region and improves affinity
IL-4 drives IgE, IFN-gamma drives IgG, TGF-beta and IL-5 drive IgA

note: Review: IgG1 changed to IgE, because IL-4 drives IgE (and IgG4) in humans; IL-4 to IgG1 is the mouse pattern.

stem: A 12-year-old boy has had recurrent pneumococcal pneumonia and otitis media since age 1 year. He has no tonsils on examination, his blood counts are normal, and B cells are nearly absent on flow cytometry. Serum protein electrophoresis is performed.
oneliner: 12M + recurrent pneumococcal pneumonia and otitis + no tonsils + near-absent B cells → which electrophoresis band is reduced?
ask: Which electrophoresis band is most reduced?

whyNot.A: Made by the liver and **normal** here; low albumin suggests liver or protein loss
whyNot.B: Mostly **alpha-1 antitrypsin**, unaffected by a B-cell defect
whyNot.C: Haptoglobin, ceruloplasmin and **alpha-2 macroglobulin**, not immunoglobulins
whyNot.D: Holds **transferrin** and complement, which are produced normally

why: **Recurrent encapsulated-bacteria infections with absent B cells and no tonsils** in a boy is **X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia**. Immunoglobulins migrate in the **gamma** region, so the band is **flat**. Albumin runs ahead, then **alpha-1 (AAT)**, **alpha-2 (haptoglobin, ceruloplasmin)**, **beta (transferrin, complement)**, and **gamma**.
chain: BTK defect stops B cells maturing
No plasma cells, no immunoglobulin production
Immunoglobulins normally migrate in the gamma band
Gamma band is flat
Other bands are unchanged

idea.rule: Serum protein electrophoresis: albumin, alpha-1, alpha-2, beta, gamma; immunoglobulins sit in the gamma band.
also: Myeloma: a sharp M spike in the gamma region
Nephrotic syndrome: low albumin, raised alpha-2 (macroglobulin)
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency: absent alpha-1 band
Polyclonal gamma rise: chronic infection or inflammation

stem: A 55-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus takes hydroxychloroquine. She has 2 days of fever to 38.9 C and a productive cough. ESR is 62 mm/h, CRP is markedly raised, anti-dsDNA is unchanged, C3 and C4 are normal, and urinalysis is bland.
oneliner: 55F + SLE + 2 days fever and productive cough + ESR 62 + very high CRP + stable dsDNA, normal C3 and C4, bland urine → what does the high CRP suggest?
ask: What does the markedly raised CRP most likely indicate?

whyNot.B: Would show **active urine sediment** and falling **C3 and C4**; her urine is bland and complement normal
whyNot.C: Lupus flares usually raise **ESR** but **not CRP**; her **dsDNA is stable and complement normal**
whyNot.D: Needs **neuropsychiatric** features, absent here, and CRP is usually normal
whyNot.E: Would present with **clots** or pregnancy loss, not fever and cough

why: **CRP** is an **acute-phase protein made by the liver under IL-6** that opsonizes bacteria. In SLE, type I interferon **suppresses CRP**, so flares usually raise **ESR but not CRP**. A **very high CRP with fever and cough** therefore points to **infection** (or serositis), not lupus activity.
chain: IL-6 from infected tissue acts on the liver
CRP rises sharply (opsonin)
Lupus flare alone leaves CRP low (interferon effect)
ESR rises in both
High CRP with fever therefore means infection

idea.rule: In SLE, a high ESR with a normal CRP fits a flare; a high CRP suggests infection or serositis.
also: IL-6 drives liver production of CRP, fibrinogen and hepcidin
CRP rises within hours and falls fast, while ESR lags
Infection is a leading cause of death in SLE
Serositis can raise CRP in lupus

stem: A 28-year-old man has a tender, swollen index finger 2 days after a splinter, and an abscess is forming. Neutrophils are leaving the blood at this site, first rolling along the vessel wall and then sticking firmly to it. Resident tissue macrophages near the splinter are releasing cytokines that switch the local venular endothelium into an adhesive state.
oneliner: 28M + splinter abscess + neutrophils rolling then sticking in local venules + macrophage cytokine → which cytokine?
ask: Which macrophage-derived cytokine most directly makes the endothelium display the rolling adhesion molecule (E-selectin)?

whyNot.A: Macrophages release IL-10 to **dampen** inflammation; it does not switch endothelium on
whyNot.B: A **T-cell (Th2)** cytokine, not one made by the resident macrophages in this scenario
whyNot.D: Made mainly by **Th1 and NK cells** and acts on macrophages; it is not the early macrophage signal that turns on selectins
whyNot.E: Mainly **anti-inflammatory and fibrogenic**; it does not drive early leukocyte adhesion

why: Macrophages that sense bacteria through Toll-like receptors release **TNF-α and IL-1**. These cytokines make venular endothelium **express E-selectin** and raise ICAM-1 and VCAM-1. Leukocyte ligands bind selectins to cause **rolling**, then integrins bind ICAM-1 for **firm adhesion**.
chain: Bacteria from the splinter engage Toll-like receptors on macrophages
Macrophages release TNF-α and IL-1
Venular endothelium expresses E-selectin and more ICAM-1/VCAM-1
Neutrophil sialyl-Lewis X binds selectins: rolling
Integrin–ICAM-1 binding: firm adhesion, then transmigration

idea.rule: TNF-α and IL-1 turn endothelium adhesive: selectins for rolling, ICAM-1/VCAM-1 for sticking.
also: Histamine and thrombin move P-selectin to the surface within minutes
Sialyl-Lewis X on leukocytes is the ligand for selectins
LFA-1 and Mac-1 integrins bind ICAM-1 (defective in leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1)
TNF-α also causes fever and, in excess, septic shock

stem: A 17-year-old boy has had a second episode of meningococcal meningitis. Serum testing shows no total hemolytic activity through the classical route (CH50) and none through the alternative route (AH50), while his C3 and C4 levels are normal. Consider how the three complement activation routes (classical, lectin, alternative) feed into the part of the cascade he cannot complete.
oneliner: 17M + recurrent meningococcal meningitis + CH50 and AH50 both absent + normal C3, C4 → where do the pathways converge?
ask: Upstream of his defect, cleavage of which component is the first step shared by all three pathways?

whyNot.A: First component of the **classical pathway only**; the lectin and alternative routes bypass it
whyNot.C: Used by the **classical and lectin** routes, not the alternative route, so it cannot be common to all three
whyNot.D: This is the **membrane attack complex**, the downstream part he lacks, not the point where the routes meet

answer: C3 (cleaved into C3a and C3b by the C3 convertase)
why: All three pathways build a **C3 convertase** that cleaves **C3 into C3a and C3b**. C3b joins the convertase to form the **C5 convertase**, which starts assembly of **C5b-C9**. Without the terminal components both CH50 and AH50 are absent, and **Neisseria**, which depend on membrane attack complex killing, cause recurrent infection.
chain: Classical (C1, C4, C2), lectin (MBL) and alternative (C3, B, D) routes each form a C3 convertase
C3 is cleaved into C3a and C3b
C3b joins the convertase to make the C5 convertase
C5b recruits C6, C7, C8 and C9 to form the membrane attack complex
His terminal components are missing: no lysis of Neisseria

idea.rule: Classical, lectin and alternative pathways differ at the start but all converge on C3 cleavage; only C5b-C9 makes the lytic pore.
also: C3 deficiency: severe recurrent infections with encapsulated bacteria
C5-C9 deficiency: recurrent Neisseria
C1 inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, not infection
C3a and C5a are anaphylatoxins; C3b is the main opsonin

stem: A 35-year-old woman with an asthma exacerbation is given a high dose of prednisone. She has no fever or infection. A complete blood count the next day is compared with one taken before the dose.
oneliner: 35F + asthma flare + high-dose prednisone + no fever or infection → which white cell set the next day?
ask: Which set of changes best describes her blood counts?

whyNot.A: This is the **opposite** of the glucocorticoid effect
whyNot.B: Glucocorticoids **lower** lymphocytes and eosinophils, sequestering them and inducing apoptosis
whyNot.C: Neutrophils **rise** because adhesion to the vessel wall is reduced
whyNot.E: Eosinophils **fall** on steroids, which is why they are used in asthma and eosinophilic disease

answer: Neutrophils up; lymphocytes and eosinophils down
why: Glucocorticoids reduce **adhesion molecule** expression, so neutrophils leave the marginated pool and **demarginate** into circulation, raising the count. They also cause **lymphocyte and eosinophil** apoptosis and redistribution, so these counts fall.
chain: Glucocorticoid dose
Neutrophil adhesion molecules decrease, cells demarginate
Neutrophilia
Lymphocytes and eosinophils undergo apoptosis and sequestration
Lymphopenia and eosinopenia

idea.rule: Steroids: neutrophils up, lymphocytes and eosinophils down.
also: Adrenal insufficiency: eosinophilia and lymphocytosis
Cushing syndrome: neutrophilia, lymphopenia
Epinephrine also demarginates neutrophils
Steroid-treated leukemia or lymphoma: lymphocytes fall
